headline: Module 2 Complete — Reconnaissance & Footprinting
message:
On day five of the Meridian Financial engagement, Maya sent the reconnaissance report.

Fourteen findings. Four critical (two remediated during the engagement). Five high. Four medium. One low. Every finding had a source, a timestamp, evidence, a severity rating, and a recommended action. The report was twenty-three pages including screenshots and evidence. It had been built over five days — one finding at a time, documented the moment it was discovered.

James read it cover to cover before active testing started on Monday. He said one thing: 'I know exactly where to start.'

That is what a reconnaissance report is supposed to do.

Look at where you started five missions ago. In Mission 1, you learned that the internet never forgets — that digital footprints accumulate over time and are permanent in ways most people never consider. You learned to read those footprints: old cached pages, historical registrations, indexed documents from years ago.

In Mission 2, you learned domain intelligence — that a domain name is not a website, it is a key to a public record system. You learned WHOIS and what a registration date means. You learned the DNS resolution hierarchy from your browser to the root servers. You learned that MX records tell you who handles email, that NS records tell you who manages DNS, that TXT records contain an organisation's complete cloud vendor list, and that DMARC tells you whether a domain can be spoofed.

In Mission 3, you went deeper into DNS. You learned all eight record types and what each one reveals. You learned about zone transfers and why a misconfigured nameserver hands over the complete building blueprint. You learned about subdomain enumeration — wordlist brute force, Certificate Transparency, the forgotten development servers that sit in DNS long after everyone stopped thinking about them.

In Mission 4, you opened Google — and realised it was something completely different from what you thought. You learned that Googlebot has been crawling the public internet for years, collecting everything it finds, and building an index that professionals query with surgical precision. You learned to find exposed documents, open directories, admin portals, and unauthenticated API endpoints — all without touching a single target system. You learned that robots.txt is a disclosure risk, not a protection. You learned to read document metadata and extract the hidden story of who made it and when.

And in this mission, you learned how it all connects. The SCOUT framework. The five phases. The intelligence profile. The attack surface map. The professional standards that govern scope, escalation, documentation, and the line between passive research and active testing.

You know how a professional starts a penetration test.

Module 3 is where that preparation pays off.

Until now, everything has been passive. You have been reading, querying, observing. You have not sent a single packet to a target's system. You have not made a single connection that left a log entry. You have built a complete picture of an organisation's internet presence from the outside — using only what they made public, deliberately or accidentally.

In Module 3 — Scanning and Enumeration — that changes. You will send your first Nmap packet. You will connect to open ports. You will fingerprint services and operating systems. You will discover what is actually running on those systems, not what a banner claimed months ago when Shodan crawled it. You will make the attack surface map concrete and specific.

The reconnaissance you just learned is what makes that scanning targeted. You already know which systems to scan first. You already know which ports are worth investigating. You already know the technology era you are dealing with and the attack paths most likely to exist.

Everything from here is active. And active starts with a purpose — because you built the map.

badgesUnlocked.description: Completed Module 2: Reconnaissance & Footprinting — mastered the complete professional passive reconnaissance methodology. Can build a structured intelligence profile from WHOIS, DNS enumeration, Google Dorking, and OSINT. Applies the SCOUT framework, prioritises attack surfaces into four tiers, understands immediate escalation standards, and knows when passive reconnaissance is complete and active testing can begin.

nextSteps: Module 03: Scanning and Enumeration — your first active techniques. Nmap port scanning, service fingerprinting, OS detection, and banner grabbing. The passive attack surface map meets the active scanner — and you already know which systems to start with.
Optional: Complete the Reconnaissance Methodology Lab — applying the full SCOUT framework hands-on builds the professional instincts that no amount of reading alone can produce

Review: The complete Module 2 cheat sheets are your playbook going forward. The SCOUT framework, the DNS enumeration sequence, the Google Dorking operator list, and the attack surface priority matrix appear in every professional engagement from here.
